title: API 653 Training in Newark: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for New York Harbor tank inspectors: Bayonne, Carteret, Linden and Perth Amboy terminals, N.J.A.C. 7:1E and winter tanks.
h1: API 653 Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Newark and the New York Harbor Terminals
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors in the New York Harbor terminal belt

The New Jersey side of New York Harbor is storage country. Terminals at Bayonne, Linden, Carteret and Perth Amboy, and the Bayway refinery's tank fields, sit within a short drive of Newark. The six terminal sites in the table below alone list roughly 35 million barrels between them, in figures published at different dates.

Atlantis NDT's API 653 course is self-paced and online with instructor Q&A: you enrol, begin, and work through API 653, API 650 and the other publications on your window's effectivity sheet around the terminal's own calendar. There is no Atlantis classroom in Newark. The American Petroleum Institute decides eligibility under Annex D of API 653, administers the exam in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification.

The harbor's tank farms, in their operators' published figures

The table collects figures the operators, or the agencies that regulate them, have published. Kinder Morgan's terminal sheets carry no publication date; other dates are given where the source has one.

SitePublished figuresProducts named
IMTT, Bayonne392 tanks and about 12.5 million barrels; seven deepwater ship berths and eleven barge berthsPetroleum products, ethanol, biofuels, commodity and specialty chemicals, oleochemicals, vegetable and tropical oils

Buckeye describes about 12 million barrels of storage across its New York Harbor network, and the EPA lists tank fields among the parts of the roughly 1,300-acre Bayway property. IMTT names Riverstone as its sponsor; Riverstone bought the company from Macquarie Infrastructure Corporation in a transaction IMTT says was finalised in December 2020. Tanks from about 1,200 to 300,000 barrels, heated, blanketed and refrigerated service can all share one site.

New Jersey's integrity-testing rule and the federal SPCC rule

New Jersey's discharge prevention rules define a major facility by its total combined storage: 200,000 gallons or more of hazardous substances of all kinds, or 20,000 gallons or more of hazardous substances other than petroleum. At those facilities, N.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16 sets integrity testing for aboveground storage tanks of more than 2,000 gallons:

  • Field-erected steel atmospheric tanks are tested to API 653, and shop-built steel atmospheric tanks to API 653 or SP001, on the schedules those standards set.
  • The similar-service and risk-based inspection scheduling options are not permitted for this purpose.
  • New tanks, and in the current text relocated tanks and tanks returning to service, are tested before service together with their piping up to the first valve.
  • The test report has to state the inspector's qualifications, with API or STI certification named as examples, and it is kept for the life of the tank, along with a written record of what was done about each recommendation.

The current version of the rule took effect in mid-2025 and, among other changes, extended the bar on risk-based scheduling to pressurised tanks tested under API 510. The federal Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure rule sits beside it: 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6) requires regular integrity testing of aboveground bulk containers, and EPA's August 2013 fact sheet on the subject says formal out-of-service internal inspections under API 653 are to be carried out by an API 653 certified inspector. Neither rule is examined.

Breakout tanks where the pipelines reach the harbor

The products pipelines meet the terminals here: Kinder Morgan's Carteret sheet lists receipts from Colonial lines L6 and L7, IMTT lists Buckeye, Colonial and Harbor Pipeline connections, and Colonial, owned outright by Brookfield since 2025, runs terminal-to-terminal transfers through its Linden Junction facility. A tank that an operator uses as a breakout tank for a hazardous liquid pipeline answers to 49 CFR 195.432 as well as to the state rule.

Under paragraph (a) a breakout tank gets a yearly inspection, no more than 15 months apart, unless it is one of the tanks that paragraphs (b) and (c) send to API 653 or API 510 instead. Paragraph (b) covers atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks through API 653 minus its section 6.4.3, which means risk-based procedures cannot set their internal inspection interval; paragraph (c) sends tanks built to API 2510 to section 6 of API 510. PHMSA published a proposed rule in June 2026 that would let operators use risk-based methods for breakout tanks, and until a final rule appears the existing text applies. API 653 is examined; Part 195 is not.

Products that decide the damage: ethanol, heated oils and chemicals

The API 653 Body of Knowledge issued for the 2027 windows names ten RP 571 mechanisms, and harbor service gives a working example of most of them:

  • Ethanol stress corrosion cracking. At a site such as Kinder Morgan's Linden terminal, which lists ethanol as its only commodity, this is the mechanism to study first; cracking favours welds and other high-stress areas, so crack detection matters more there than thickness readings.
  • Corrosion under insulation. Heated and insulated tanks, which go with the product heating several terminals offer, can hide shell corrosion behind cladding, particularly near the bottom course and wherever water collects.
  • Caustic corrosion, caustic stress corrosion cracking and sulfuric acid corrosion. Chemical storage at the larger terminals, and acid service of the kind the NJIT study attributes to the sulfuric acid regeneration business in the Bayway complex, bring these mechanisms into a tank inspector's work.
  • Microbiologically influenced corrosion and concentration cell corrosion. Water and sludge beneath fuels and biodiesel feed product-side pitting of floors and lower shell.
  • Soil and atmospheric corrosion. On low-lying harbor ground the soil side of a bottom relies on cathodic protection (RP 651), linings (RP 652) protect the product side, and salt air works on roofs, wind girders and the shell-to-bottom chime.
  • Brittle fracture. North Jersey winters make this one worth a section of its own.

Winter on the Arthur Kill: brittle fracture and the Section 5 screen

The Body of Knowledge lists the risk of failure due to brittle fracture among its API 653 topics, and Section 5 of the standard gives the screening procedure. It works as a series of questions:

  1. Was the tank built to the toughness requirements of API 650's seventh edition or later, or do impact tests on representative shell plate show adequate toughness? If so, the risk is treated as minimal.
  2. Is the original nominal thickness of the thickest shell plate 0.5 in or less? Then the risk is minimal, provided a Section 4 evaluation has been carried out.
  3. Does the shell run at a metal temperature of 60°F or above? API 653 records no known brittle fracture failures at shell metal temperatures at or above that line.
  4. If not, does the plate's material group and thickness fall in the safe region of the exemption curves, with Figure 5.2 used for carbon steel of unknown toughness?
  5. If not, has the tank operated at its maximum liquid level at the lowest one-day mean temperature without failure, as tank records and weather data show?
  6. If not, the owner restricts the liquid level, the minimum metal temperature or the product specific gravity, runs a hydrostatic test, or commissions further analysis.

Where a harbor tank has steel of unknown toughness, thick lower courses and winter shell temperatures well below 60°F, the assessment goes past the first screens, and after a change to a heavier product or colder service the earlier operating history no longer carries over. In the exam, expect to be given a thickness, a temperature and a material and asked which region of the curve applies.

Worked example: scattered pits on a first shell course

Shell pitting evaluation is on the current Body of Knowledge's calculation list. API 653 lets widely scattered pits be ignored only if two conditions hold: no pit leaves a remaining thickness below half the minimum acceptable shell thickness, exclusive of corrosion allowance; and the pit dimensions measured along any vertical line add up to no more than 2 in within an 8 in length.

Given: a field-erected tank 150 ft in diameter with a maximum liquid level of 48 ft, storing diesel at a specific gravity of 0.85; allowable stress for the first course S = 23,600 psi, as given in the question; the pits are well away from welds, so E = 1.0.

Step 1, minimum course thickness. For a whole course, tmin = 2.6(H − 1)DG / SE = 2.6 × 47 × 150 × 0.85 / 23,600 = 0.66 in. Half of that is 0.33 in. For a locally thinned area the formula instead uses H measured from the bottom of the area to the maximum liquid level, without subtracting a foot.

Step 2, the deepest pit. Ultrasonic readings at the deepest pit show 0.36 in remaining. That is above 0.33 in, so the first condition holds.

Step 3, the vertical line. Three pits lie on one vertical line within an 8 in length, measuring 0.75 in, 0.70 in and 0.65 in along that line. Their sum is 2.10 in, more than 2 in, so the second condition fails and the pits cannot be ignored.

Step 4, what follows. The area must now be evaluated as a corroded area by averaging over the critical length, repaired, or the fill height reduced. If cleaning shows the middle pit is really 0.45 in long, the sum becomes 1.85 in and the pits can be ignored after all, which is why exam questions turn on reading the dimensions carefully.

Becoming an API 653 inspector from a harbor terminal job

Annex D of API 653 combines education with tank experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency, and every route includes at least one year supervising or performing tank inspection. A BS in engineering or technology needs one year of inspection; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years of tank experience; a high school diploma needs three; no formal education needs five or more.

  • NDT technicians who run UT shell surveys, MFL floor scans or weld examinations on terminal tanks are already doing inspection activities; if you need the method qualifications first, see NDT training for Newark candidates.
  • Terminal maintenance and operations staff build tank experience through operation and repair, but still need the inspection year.
  • Tank welders and erectors bring construction and repair experience.
  • Engineers at terminal operators can qualify on the degree route once they have a year of inspection work.

New Jersey's test report must state the inspector's qualifications, and the rule's first example is API certification. Full rules are on the API 653 certification page.

Studying API 653 around a terminal's tank-cleaning season

Tank work at a harbor terminal follows the commercial calendar: tanks come out of service for cleaning, internal inspection and repairs when the operator can spare their capacity. A self-paced course lets you use the quiet months. A workable sequence:

  1. Read API 653 once through, then RP 575 and the ten RP 571 mechanisms.
  2. Work the Body of Knowledge calculations one by one: corrosion rates and intervals, joint efficiencies, maximum fill height, shell openings and hot taps, settlement and survey points, impact testing, existing and reconstructed shell thickness, corroded areas and pitting, bottom plates, replacement plates and lap-welded patches.
  3. Learn your way around API 650 as a PDF, because the open-book half sends you there for welding, testing and design tables.
  4. Add ASME Sections V and IX for the NDE and welding questions, then sit timed practice papers.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a harbor terminal network

An operator with tanks at several harbor sites, or an inspection company serving them, can enrol a group on one quote; fees are quoted on request. Each candidate studies at their own pace with instructor Q&A and applies to API individually for the window they choose. A group can mix a technician who already runs floor scans, an engineer on the degree route and a maintenance supervisor working toward the inspection year, each starting from where they are. API 570 for the same people's dock and transfer piping work can be quoted alongside.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in person near Newark?
faq.a: No. The course runs online and self-paced, with an instructor answering questions as you study, and Atlantis has no classroom near Newark or anywhere else. You fit the work around terminal shifts and outages and take the examination itself in person at a Prometric test centre; Prometric lists test centres in and around Newark, and you choose one when you schedule within API's window.

faq.q: Does New Jersey's discharge prevention rule require an API 653 certified inspector?
faq.a: N.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16 requires field-erected steel atmospheric tanks at major facilities to be integrity tested to API 653 and the report to state the inspector's qualifications, giving API or STI certification as examples. Separately, EPA's SPCC fact sheet says formal API 653 internal inspections are to be done by an API 653 certified inspector. Check the current rule text and your facility's plan for the exact requirement at your site.

faq.q: Can a harbor terminal use API 653's risk-based inspection option in New Jersey?
faq.a: Not to schedule integrity tests of tanks covered by N.J.A.C. 7:1E-2.16, which excludes API 653's similar-service and risk-based scheduling, and not to set the internal interval of a breakout tank under 49 CFR 195.432. You still need the RBI provisions for the exam, and a terminal can use risk ranking to decide what to examine and where within the schedule the rules fix.

faq.q: Our Linden terminal stores only ethanol. What should I study first?
faq.a: Begin with ethanol stress corrosion cracking in RP 571, which the Body of Knowledge lists, and with the parts of RP 575 that deal with finding cracks rather than thinning. Then move on to the shell and bottom calculations every candidate needs. Ethanol tanks still corrode in ordinary ways, so floor and shell thickness work matters, but crack detection at welds is what sets ethanol service apart from fuel oil.

faq.q: Are pressurised tanks at a harbor terminal API 653 tanks?
faq.a: No. API 653 is written for atmospheric steel storage tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, API 12C. Pressurised tanks built to API 2510 are inspected under API 510: 49 CFR 195.432 says so for breakout tanks, and New Jersey's integrity-testing rule sends pressurised tanks to API 510 or ASME Section VIII. If your terminal has both kinds, API 510 is the certificate that covers the pressurised side.

faq.q: Does the API 653 exam test New Jersey tank rules or Part 195?
faq.a: No. The exam covers the documents on the effectivity sheet for your window: API 653, API 650, RP 575, the listed RP 571 mechanisms, RP 577, the two named sections of RP 576, RP 651, RP 652, the listed articles of ASME Section V, and Section IX. N.J.A.C. 7:1E and 49 CFR 195.432 decide how tanks are scheduled at work; keep them out of your exam answers.

faq.q: I do UT shell surveys for an inspection contractor in Carteret. Does that count toward API 653?
faq.a: It can count as inspection activity if you do it while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, and you describe it accurately on the application. How much you need depends on your education: one year with a BS in engineering or technology, two with a two-year degree, three with a high school diploma, five or more without formal education. API verifies the experience and makes the decision.
